prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B006 alone, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having reread the full exchange, the scientific case is the same one all six of us made. It is a complete arc from proglucagon processing and the active truncated peptide, through glucose-dependent insulinotropic action in humans and the wider biology of satiety, gastric emptying and tissue effects, to therapies backed by large randomized outcome trials. The remaining open question is whom to credit, not whether the discovery is mature. The three names carry three discrete, citable discoveries: Holst on human incretin physiology and GLP-1 secretion, Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form, and Drucker on receptor biology, tissue actions and the translational concept. A Physiology or Medicine citation should be anchored on discovery of the hormone's biology and its active molecular form, and the citation wording can say plainly that the downstream therapy rests on that discovery. I considered a second prize part and do not propose one this year: B006 already uses all three names, and I would not drop any of them for B039 or B004.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested, Habener is outside the supplied names, and the committee cannot adjudicate that from these files. Any physiology-centred trio omits Knudsen, whose albumin-binding acylation gave liraglutide and semaglutide their durable action, and could be read as honouring the science while skipping the person whose work reached patients. If the committee were to conclude that the documentary record on the active peptide is too uncertain to support naming Mojsov, the Knudsen configuration would become the more defensible one and I would reconsider; I do not think that has been shown. A second, narrower risk is that the citation overclaims, so I would keep the wording to physiology and the active form and not claim the whole therapeutic chain.

responses.point: Argues that Knudsen's albumin-binding acylation is the step that made the drug class usable, that the committee should state its translation principle openly, and that the prize should not be read as favouring industrial design over discovery or the reverse.
responses.response: I accept the request to state a principle, and mine is this: a Physiology or Medicine prize should reward discoveries that define the biology and the molecule, and the citation may acknowledge the downstream therapy without crediting the engineering program. That principle can be applied consistently to B004 and B040, where it would likewise favour discovery of the mechanism or concept over later optimisation, though I admit CAR-T design work is closer to discovery than acylation chemistry is. Your point that the acylation was decisive is true, but it is one contribution inside a large industrial effort, and a single named representative of that effort is arbitrary in a way that the identification of the active peptide is not. I therefore stay with Mojsov, while conceding that your configuration is defensible if the committee rules the peptide-priority record unusable.

responses.point: Moved off Mojsov because naming her without Habener makes the peptide-identification chapter hard to defend, and asks that the citation name both physiology and translation. Also suggests cGAS-STING deserves a higher position.
responses.response: Your Habener objection is the strongest argument against my trio, and I have weighed it seriously. Still, a missing name that cannot be added under the cap argues for careful wording, not for removing a discrete contribution we can name. Dropping Mojsov does not solve the Habener problem, it only moves the omitted credit elsewhere, so my citation speaks of identification of the active form and does not claim a first-identification priority. On translation, I would rather acknowledge it in the citation's final clause than credit it with a name. On cGAS-STING I remain where I was: the Chen and Barber mechanism is clean and I take your point about its relevance to self-DNA-driven autoimmunity, but with no validated therapy and disappointing STING modulators, I would not put it above B039 this year.

responses.point: Wants the committee to state openly that the physiology-centred choice leaves out Knudsen and Habener, so the citation does not claim the whole therapeutic chain, and lists the same B039 alternative with a concern about a second prize part forcing removal of a GLP-1 laureate.
responses.response: I agree and have tightened my citation accordingly: it names the physiology of GLP-1 and the identity of its active form, and describes the therapies as made possible by that work, not as its object. I would support a short explanatory note from the committee that the long-acting analogue program and earlier peptide work by others are recognised but outside the three-name limit. On your second point, I share your reading that a B039 second part would force dropping a GLP-1 name, and I see no GLP-1 name I would drop. That is why I keep B039 as my first alternative for a future year and not as a companion part now.

responses.point: Moved to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, willing to hear the case for B039 as a second part but needing to know which GLP-1 name would be dropped, and rates B039 clinical consequence as still developing.
responses.response: Your question is the right test and my answer is that I would drop none, so I do not propose B039 as a second part. On the chair's request for documentary evidence on the Mojsov and Habener question, I still cannot supply it, since I am working from recalled history and the files give no primary record. I therefore state my position as conditional: Mojsov stands unless the committee obtains evidence that undermines her claim to the active-peptide identification, in which case I would move to Knudsen and amend the citation. I agree with your reading that B039 has the cleanest attribution but that its clinical consequence is still developing, which is why it stays an alternative.

responses.point: Accepts the physiology-centred trio but would keep the citation worded around the physiology and the active peptide, not around any single first-identification claim, and would accept Knudsen for Mojsov if the citation named the therapeutic achievement.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and have kept it that way. On your swap condition, I think it is a coherent fallback, but it changes the prize's meaning, from discovery of the hormone's biology to physiology plus drug design, and the committee should make that choice openly and not as a drafting convenience. I would not accept the swap merely to name the therapeutic achievement, since a citation clause can acknowledge it without a name attached.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record supports crediting Mojsov for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and whether Habener's omission from the credited names is acceptable. This is the one fact that could change my configuration.
Whether the committee wants to reward discovery of the physiology and active form only, or also the drug-design step, given the three-person cap.
Whether the B004 and B040 cases, if they return in a later year, would be judged by the same translation principle as B006.
I am relying on recalled history for priority questions and have not verified them from primary documents.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I disclosed in round 1 that I have co-authored with Sandberg, Frisen and Betsholtz, and as a co-author of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper I have a scientific connection in a different field. None involves B006 or any other shortlisted candidate, and I disclose no new connections in round 2.
